title: Helping the Old
text:
I was in the bank line today

when the old man in front of me

dropped his glasses (fortunately

inside the case)

and I saw how hard it was for him

to bend down

and I said: "wait, let me

pick them up for you"

but while I was picking them up

he dropped his cane,

a cane

beautiful, black, polished,

and I gave him back the glasses

then went for the cane

and the old man regained his balance

when I gave it to him.

He said nothing,

only smiled at me.

Then he turned

forward.

And I stayed behind him waiting

my turn.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the small practical kindness and the unspoken bank-line ending.

title: It Is Very Hard to Find a Man...
text:
it is very hard to find a man

who writes poems

that do not disappoint you.

Vallejo never disappointed me that way.


some say he died

from starving so much.


whatever

his poems about the terror of being

alone

are in a sense kind and

do not

shout.


we are tired of almost all

art.

Vallejo writes like a man

and not like an

artist.

he is beyond

our understanding.


I like to think Vallejo is still

alive and walking around the

room, I find

the sound of his steps firm.

imponderable.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Bukowski's plain praise of Vallejo as a man beyond artifice.

title: Alone with Everybody
text:
The flesh covers the bone

and inside they put

a brain and

sometimes a soul,

and women throw

vases against the walls

and men drink

too much and nobody finds the other

but they keep

looking

from bed

to bed.

The flesh covers

the bone and the

flesh looks for

something more than

flesh.

There is no

possibility:

we are all trapped

by a singular

fate.

Nobody ever finds

the other.

The slums fill up

the dumps fill up

the madhouses fill up

the hospitals fill up

the graves fill up

nothing else fills up.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the flesh/bone refrain and the bleak inventory of places filling up.

title: When I Think of My Death
text:
I think of cars parked in a

parking lot

when I think of my death

I think of frying pans

when I think of my death

I think someone is making love to you

when I am not there

when I think of my death

I have trouble breathing

when I think of my death

I think of all the people waiting to die

when I think of my death

I think I will never be able to drink water again

when I think of my death

the air turns completely white

the cockroaches in my kitchen

tremble

and I think someone will have to throw

my clean and dirty underwear

very far away.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated death-thoughts and the mundane final image of discarded underwear.

title: The Wind Blows Hard Tonight...
text:
The wind blows hard tonight

And it is a cold wind

And I think of the boys

On the street.

I hope some of them have

A bottle of red wine.


When you are on the street

That is when you realize that

Everything

Has an owner

And that there are locks on

Everything.

This is how democracy works:

You take what you can,

Try to keep it

And add something

If possible.


This is also how

Dictatorship works

Only one enslaves

And the other destroys its

Disinherited.


We simply forget

Our own.


In any case

It is a wind

Hard

And cold.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the street-level comparison of democracy, dictatorship, ownership, and forgetting the dispossessed.
